entry.title: Leading the way in Greater Manchester – bringing people, nature, connectivity and growth together
entry.summary: Lucy Abram, Deputy Director of the Cheshire, Lancashire, Greater Manchester and Merseyside Team CyanLines is a bold plan to link and transform Greater Manchester’s green and blue spaces - and it's just celebrated its first birthday. This blog explores how Greater Manchester is putting nature at the heart of its …
entry.content:
Lucy Abram, Deputy Director of the Cheshire, Lancashire, Greater Manchester and Merseyside Team

CyanLines is a bold plan to link and transform Greater Manchester’s green and blue spaces - and it's just celebrated its first birthday. This blog explores how Greater Manchester is putting nature at the heart of its future growth and development, and celebrates the first year of CyanLines, an ambitious programme connecting people with nature across the city region. It explains the ways in which the city regards nature as essential infrastructure, delivering benefits that range from cleaner air and reduced flood risk to improved health, wellbeing and economic prosperity.  

Greater Manchester has long been a leader in reconnecting people with nature. Nature is not a nice-to-have or an afterthought. It is essential infrastructure.

Natural England has been working across Greater Manchester for many years, building strong partnerships with the Greater Manchester Combined Authority, local authorities and environmental NGOs. Together, we are shaping strategic plans and delivering projects that create lasting benefits for communities, nature and the local economy.

Nature cleans our air and water, reduces flood risk, stores carbon, cools our urban environments, supports food production and strengthens the economy. And importantly, access to green space improves physical and mental wellbeing, with green spaces estimated to save the NHS £2.1 billion every year by helping people live healthier lives.

Ensuring these spaces are accessible, with routes starting on people's doorsteps, is more important than ever.

As the first area in the North of England to publish the Local Nature Recovery Strategy, Greater Manchester is leading the way in working across a range of partnerships to integrate nature into the fabric of the city region. This vision goes hand-in-hand with ambitious plans for housing, world-class employment spaces, and hubs for innovation, science and technology, demonstrating that growth and nature are not competing priorities. 

The development of CyanLines is a powerful example of this ambition. By creating a connected network of nature-rich spaces linked by walking routes, canals and rivers, the project will make it easier than ever for people to experience and enjoy nature across the city.

It's ambitious. It's transformative. And if there's one thing Manchester has never been afraid of, it is thinking big. 

Celebrating One Year of CyanLines  

In September 2025, more than 600 people descended upon Aviva Studios in central Manchester to hear of a new ambitious programme that was set to transform the green and blue routes across Greater Manchester. 12-months on, crowds returned to the creative hub on the banks of the River Irwell to hear first-hand of the progress made.

Born from the minds of Tom Bloxham CBE MBE (Chair and Founder of Urban Splash) and Pete Swift (Founding Director and CEO of Planit) – and backed by the former leader of Manchester City Council and recently elected Mayor of Greater Manchester, Bev Craig, and our new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham – CyanLines is a bold initiative to create a 100-mile network of green spaces and waterways across the city region, connecting local people with the nature-rich landscape that makes Greater Manchester so unique.

Mayor of Greater Manchester and co-chair of CyanLines Bev Craig said:

“We’re on a mission to connect our green spaces with nature across Greater Manchester.

“The ambition of CyanLines to join up our green spaces, rivers and canals is a key part of our vision to create a greener, healthier and better-connected city region. It shows what we can achieve when communities, businesses and the public and voluntary sectors come together with a shared purpose.”

It is part of one of the first projects to be part funded by the Nature Towns and Cities initiative, a transformative coalition of organisations bringing nature, green infrastructure and natural heritage into communities. Salford & Manchester are one area where nearly £1 million has been awarded to create thriving nature corridors and parks to connect existing open spaces and waterways into a cohesive network.

One of the core components of CyanLines is a commitment to be led by the evidence. The CyanLabs programme pulls together key organisations – such as Natural England and academics from Greater Manchester’s Universities – to design where the next tranche of CyanLines should go, to improve nature’s recovery whilst creating more green corridors in areas of most need for the greatest health benefits. 

This week, the CyanLines coalition reconnected for the 2026 annual stakeholder event, using the one-year anniversary as a moment to celebrate the development of the four initial routes across the urban centre of Manchester and Salford. A warm reception was received from both private and public partners, celebrating this next phase and revealing two major announcements: firstly, a significant charitable grant from the Bupa Foundation to the National Trust towards Phase Two of Castlefield Viaduct. Secondly, plans for a new CyanLines route, CL5, which will significantly improve the experience of walking and wheeling to the Etihad Stadium and Co-op Live Arena from the City Centre through a series practical and nature led interventions.

As ever, it was striking to see the breadth of representation in the room; from developers who are reshaping areas of Greater Manchester to policy professionals, everyone has united under the CyanLines plan to help deliver for nature and people.

It was also a pleasure to welcome our Chair of Natural England, Tony Juniper, to Manchester, as he spoke at the annual event and ventured on a walk along CL4 earlier that day.

Tony Juniper, Chair of Natural England, said:

“This is a great example of the kind of silo-busting partnership working needed to deliver real results in actual places where people live and work. At Natural England we look forward to further collaboration, maximising benefits for wildlife as part of this inspiring people-focused vision."

Natural England are excited to continue working with CyanLines and partners on this exciting journey, and we can’t wait to see what we achieve together by the second anniversary.

entry.title: An Online Hub for Local Wildlife Sites: New Resources for a Vital 5% of England
entry.summary: By Sofía Muñoz and Scott Mitchell, Senior Specialists for Data Engagement and Analysis, Natural Capital and Ecosystem Assessment Programme This blog explains what Local Wildlife Sites (LWS) are, why they matter, and the importance of the new online hub where …
entry.content:
By Sofía Muñoz and Scott Mitchell, Senior Specialists for Data Engagement and Analysis, Natural Capital and Ecosystem Assessment Programme

This blog explains what Local Wildlife Sites (LWS) are, why they matter, and the importance of the new online hub where people can go for information about their own LWSs.

It's not only our best-known landscapes which matter for nature. Alongside designated areas like National Parks and Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs), there's a vast and often overlooked network of 44,000 places across England that matter for wildlife and for people: Local Wildlife Sites. But while Local Wildlife Sites (LWSs) are often well-known and valued locally, their potential to support nature recovery hasn't always been visible at a regional and national scale.

Today, the Wildlife Trusts are publishing a new online hub for LWSs, the result of an ambitious partnership with Natural England, made possible by funding from the UK government’s Natural Capital and Ecosystem Assessment programme. The hub brings together information from across the country to create a national picture, helping communities, planners, and policy-makers understand more about these sites.

What LWSs do for us 

LWSs don't carry the statutory protection of designations like SSSIs, but their contribution to nature and to people is significant. They’re identified at a local level by the people who know their areas best, and are selected for biodiversity and nature conservation value. Found on both public and private land, they can act as stepping stones and refuges for wildlife, help connect fragmented habitats, and provide valuable ecosystem services, from flood protection to cleaner air. Where they are accessible, they provide places for people to connect with the natural world.

A national landing page for LWSs 

The hub will serve as a national landing page for LWSs. It will raise awareness of these sites and their importance, provide accessible information to the public and existing LWS stakeholders, and signpost users to their relevant Local Wildlife Site partnership or Local Environmental Records Centre (LERC).

It also includes maps of the number and total area covered by LWSs , assembled by the Wildlife Trusts using information shared by LWS partnerships across the country. These show that LWSs cover over 750,000 hectares – over six times the area covered by National Nature Reserves, and approaching the 1,000,000+ ha covered by Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs).

Alongside the new hub, we've also updated the guidance on local sites (Local Wildlife Sites and Local Geological Sites) and best practice for selecting and managing sites. 

How will the hub be used? 

The hub will support local communities to learn about and care for these sites, better understand their value, and discover and enjoy those of them which are open to the public.

Having this evidence in one place will make it easier for LWSs to be considered in policy development at multiple scales, such as within 30by30, Local Nature Recovery Strategies, and land use planning and decision-making.

An uneven national patchwork 

One of the most striking things that this work illuminates is just how differently LWSs are distributed in different parts of the country. These regional differences will have implications for nature recovery. LWSs may be particularly important in an area where protected legal categories are sparse. In Birmingham and the Black Country, for example, although under 2% of the area is covered by SSSIs (against an average of 8% for England), a further 6.8% is covered by LWSs.

In Wiltshire, meanwhile, according to figures from the Wildlife Trusts, 75% of the county’s deciduous woodland is found in LWSs, compared with just 10% in SSSIs. While not all LWSs are in favourable condition or positive conservation management, LWSs can be of equal or higher biodiversity value than SSSIs.

Built on partnership 

This work would not have been possible without the many LWS partnerships across England who have spent years, in some cases decades, gathering and maintaining local evidence. We're enormously grateful to them, and to the local custodians of these sites, for their expertise and dedication.

The project was funded through the UK government's Natural Capital and Ecosystem Assessment programme (NCEA), Defra's largest research and development programme. NCEA is assessing England's land, freshwater and coastal ecosystems to produce a baseline of our natural assets by 2029, enabling a natural capital approach to policy and decision-making.

entry.title: Why beauty still matters: reflections on a career spent fighting for our finest landscapes
entry.summary: By Marian Spain, Chief Executive, Natural England As she nears the end of her career at Natural England, Chief Executive Marian Spain reflects on 40 years working with Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty, from their early days as planning tools …
entry.content:
By Marian Spain, Chief Executive, Natural England

As she nears the end of her career at Natural England, Chief Executive Marian Spain reflects on 40 years working with Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty, from their early days as planning tools to their evolution into today's thriving National Landscapes. She traces the milestones that shaped this journey, and marks the moment with the submission of formal orders to extend the Surrey Hills AONB and create a new National Landscape in the Yorkshire Wolds.

40 years ago, when I started my nature conservation career working across the east and south of England, National Parks weren't really part of my world so the Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty, or AONBs, became my natural allies.

Historically, AONBs were almost entirely about planning. Their job was to stop development happening in the wrong places, but there was very little positive, active management of the countryside and they were often seen as the poorer relation to National Parks. Less funding, less action, less influence.

I am very proud therefore that I at one point held a job called "Head of Finest Countryside" (even though plenty of people pointed out, quite fairly, that this was also the name of a supermarket's premium food range!). But behind the slightly awkward title was a serious responsibility: improving the management of every AONB and National Park in the country. That was the moment when we started to see local authorities begin to invest in teams to look after AONBs, and to see them not just as places to protect from harm, but as places for nature to recover and for people to enjoy.

That shift fed into the Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000, which gave AONBs statutory management plans for the first time, and created the ability to establish Conservation Boards. It was a small but important change in the law that gave these nationally significant landscapes a firmer footing.

I also worked on the designations of the New Forest and South Downs as National Parks. Those projects sparked long debates about whether other AONBs needed to be "upgraded" to fulfil their potential too. Whatever the answer, the conversation itself pushed everyone to try harder.

It was always clear to me that AONBs were never second best. The legislation is unambiguous: it sets exactly the same standard of natural beauty for an AONB as for a National Park.  The bodies that look after AONBs were not bound by formal planning and other duties and governance as National Park Authorities are, nor did they have the same resources, so they could (and often had to be) entrepreneurial and innovative and build partnerships that reached wide and far. Necessity became a strength.

Then came the Landscapes Review chaired by Julian Glover, which asked hard questions about whether our system of protected landscapes was fit for the 21st century. Natural England contributed evidence throughout, and its recommendations have shaped much of what has followed.

Today, we have AONBs rebranded as National Landscapes, and a National Landscapes Association that champions them and pushes all of them towards the highest standards. We have the Protected Landscapes Partnership that brings National Trails, National Landscapes and National Parks together as one family. That means they work collectively on projects that transcend their boundaries, such as the “Big Chalk” project and Coastal Wildbelt.

That new vigour and ambition and collective effort is also being recognised through new designations: National Landscapes, as they have evolved to be, are as relevant today as they were the concept was first established in law in 1949.

When I joined Natural England in 2018, one of my first jobs was to sign the Order designating an extension to the Suffolk Coast and Heaths AONB. It feels fitting that, as I approach the end of my role as CEO here and the last stage of my 40-year career in nature, that I have last week with the NE Chair signed the Orders that contribute towards the potential creation/extension of two more National Landscapes. Today (7 September 2026) marks the submission of the formal orders to the Secretary of State seeking to extend Surrey Hills AONB and seeking a brand new AONB in the Yorkshire Wolds.

Whilst those landscapes are not designated unless or until the SoS confirms the decision, today, the whole family of National Landscapes are delivering on the ground in ways that would have seemed unimaginable when I started out.

Take Heathland Connections in the Surrey Hills, restoring and reconnecting fragmented heathland habitats so that wildlife can move and thrive across a landscape rather than being confined to isolated pockets. Or the Farming in Protected Landscapes scheme, which has given farmers right across our National Landscapes practical support and funding to farm sustainably, proving that food production and nature recovery can go hand in hand.

And then there's the simple, profound fact that millions of people visit these landscapes - including the Yorkshire Wolds which is home to the Yorkshire Wolds National Trail - every year for their health and wellbeing, finding space to breathe, to walk, to think. National Landscapes are places that are valued and protected not just for their beauty but are managed and promoted for everything they give us.

A landscape's work is never finished

Whatever comes next for our landscapes, I know they are in good hands. The people who care for them, who campaign for them, and who simply walk through them and are quietly changed by what they see, will make sure of that. It has been the privilege of my working life to stand alongside them.

Further information on the Yorkshire Wolds project is available at Yorkshire Wolds Designation Project

Further information on the Surrey Hills project is available at Surrey Hills National Landscape (AONB) Variation Project Second Consultation - Defra - Citizen Space

entry.title: Tony and Marian make the case for nature to Parliament's Environmental Audit Committee
entry.summary: This blog is a summary of Marian Spain and Tony Juniper's appearance in front of the Environmental Audit Committee, and reflections on their time in office. Natural England's Chair Tony Juniper and Chief Executive Marian Spain appeared before Parliament's Environmental …
entry.content:
This blog is a summary of Marian Spain and Tony Juniper's appearance in front of the Environmental Audit Committee, and reflections on their time in office.

Natural England's Chair Tony Juniper and Chief Executive Marian Spain appeared before Parliament's Environmental Audit Committee this week, reflecting on the organisation's achievements over recent years and making a strong case for why nature must remain at the heart of the country's future. 

The special session in the Houses of Parliament gave Marian and Tony the opportunity to look back at their time leading Natural England, while answering questions from MPs on some of the biggest issues facing nature and the organisation today.

Over almost two hours, the discussion ranged widely: from the condition of protected sites and species recovery to planning reform, water quality, climate change, resourcing and the role a healthy natural environment plays in economic growth and national security.

One message ran consistently through the session: nature is not a barrier to the things the country needs to achieve. It is fundamental to achieving them.

Looking back at how far we've come 

Tony opened the session by reflecting on the transformation Natural England has undergone since he and Marian began working together in 2019.

He highlighted the development of a much clearer strategic direction for the organisation, increased investment and a renewed confidence in Natural England and its role.

He also pointed to the breadth of work delivered over that period: supporting the development of Environmental Land Management and Landscape Recovery; finding new approaches to enable development while protecting nature; tackling nutrient pollution; expanding National Nature Reserves; recovering species including beavers and white-tailed eagles; connecting more people with nature; and delivering major national trails.

Marian reflected on how this work has culminated in Natural England's current strategy, Recovering Nature for Growth, Health and Security, and the shift it represents in how the organisation talks about its mission.

Nature, she told the Committee, should not be viewed simply as something that needs protecting. Healthy and resilient ecosystems provide essential services on which our economy, health and security depend.

Marian and Tony's message to those who will lead Natural England in the future was clear: keep pushing in that direction, and keep making the case for nature as essential national infrastructure, rather than a "nice to have."

Nature and growth: moving beyond the false choice 

A significant part of the discussion focused on economic growth and the persistent suggestion that protecting nature can stand in its way.

Both Marian and Tony strongly challenged that premise.

Marian stressed that Natural England recognises the country needs new homes, clean energy and infrastructure. The organisation's role is not to prevent that development, but to help ensure it happens in the most nature-friendly way possible, protecting the natural systems that the economy itself ultimately depends upon.

Tony described the idea that the country must choose between economic development and nature as a "false choice," pointing to evidence that investment in nature can create economic value and make communities and infrastructure more resilient.

Wetlands, woodlands, healthy coastlines and other natural assets, he argued, need to be thought about in much the same way as other infrastructure: investments that deliver a return for society.

Preparing for a changing climate 

Following one of the hottest summers on record, the Committee also explored the impact of climate change and how nature can help the country adapt.

The discussion highlighted the role of green spaces, trees, water and other nature-based solutions in cooling communities, managing flood risk and making places more resilient. 

Marian also drew attention to the inequality in access to nature and green space, and how communities with the least access can often be among those most exposed to the impacts of extreme heat.

Programmes such as Nature Towns and Cities demonstrate how investment in greener places can simultaneously support climate resilience, people's wellbeing and local economic growth.

A reflection of the whole organisation 

While this session focused on Marian and Tony's leadership, many of the achievements discussed are ultimately the result of the expertise, commitment and hard work of Natural England colleagues across the country.

From people working with farmers and land managers to those advising on planning and infrastructure; from scientists and specialists to colleagues working on species recovery, protected sites, access, green infrastructure and partnerships, the session provided a powerful reminder of the extraordinary breadth of what Natural England does.

Closing the hearing, Committee Chair Toby Perkins MP thanked Marian and Tony not only for their evidence, but for their contribution to Natural England over the past seven years.

As Marian prepares to leave Natural England at the end of September and Tony approaches the end of his term as Chair next year, this session provided an opportunity to reflect on what has been achieved, but also on the scale of the task still ahead.

The central message was perhaps the simplest one of all: recovering nature isn't separate from delivering the future the country needs.

It is one of the foundations on which that future depends.

entry.title: Explore More for Less: Affordable South East Nature Days Out
entry.summary: This summer, if you’re looking for fun and accessible days out that are low-cost, then we have you covered. Not only is spending time in nature great for your wellbeing, it can also be great for your bank balance. Here are our suggestions for …
entry.content:
This summer, if you’re looking for fun and accessible days out that are low-cost, then we have you covered. Not only is spending time in nature great for your wellbeing, it can also be great for your bank balance. Here are our suggestions for our favourite affordable days out in the South East!   

Whether you're after a gentle walk or a long trek, wonderful wildlife or ancient history, the South East has it all. It's tough to narrow it down, but here are some of our favourite days out for you to enjoy!

The King Charles III England Coast Path at Chichester Harbour 

Enjoy a stretch of the King Charles III England Coast Path around Thorney Island, taking in stunning views of Chichester Harbour – all within reach of Chichester and Portsmouth.  

This 8-mile route begins in the picturesque village of Emsworth and ends at Southbourne, though can be completed in either direction, and passes by special saltmarshes, mudflats and dune habitats. The fully waymarked coast path offers the chance to spot seals, coastal wildflowers and birds including terns, redshanks, curlews and ospreys. Remember, if seal or birdwatching at the coast make sure to keep your distance and not cause any disturbance!

From Emsworth you can join the coast path at Queen Street, on the eastern side of the island you can join at Prinsted Lane in Prinsted. If you fancy an even bigger challenge this stretch forms part of over 200 miles of coast path that is now open across Hampshire & Sussex! 

Please be aware that Thorney Island is an active army base. There are two security gates on either side of the island where you will be required to use an intercom system to gain onward access. Always check the National Trails website in advance of your walk to check for any temporary MOD closure notices. 

Getting there: You can catch the train from Chichester or Portsmouth to Emsworth. If you're doing the full 8-mile stretch, catch the train home from Southbourne.

Hindhead Commons, part of the Wealden Heaths National Nature Reserve (National Trust) 

Across Surrey, Hampshire & West Sussex is a 2,440 hectare patchwork of some of England's most important ancient heathlands - the Wealden Heaths National Nature Reserve.  

Hindhead Commons & the Devil's Punch Bowl, one of twenty sites across Wealden Heaths, is the perfect spot to enjoy what the NNR has to offer. Devil's Punch Bowl offers spectacular views of the colourful heath landscape. Named for the local legend of the Devil scooping and throwing dirt at Thor, the Punch Bowl has an onsite cafe with toilet facilities and is a short step-free walk from a car park and bus stop.

Hindhead Commons is home to a well waymarked walking routes from which you may see sunbathing reptiles, including sand lizards and adders, blooming heather plants, and if you're lucky, and visit near dusk, the rare nightjar bird.

With the ongoing hot and dry weather, please remember to act responsibly while in natural spaces. This NNR's heathland is especially vulnerable to wildfires, so please do not light fires or BBQs. 

Getting there: Take the number 19 bus from Haslemere Railway Station. Haslemere is a short train journey from both Godalming and Guildford.

Mount Caburn National Nature Reserve near Lewes 

Take in spectacular views of the South Downs from Mount Caburn National Nature Reserve - a  short trip from Brighton.  

Used since the Iron Age as a base for fortifications, the south facing chalk hill and valley of Mount Caburn's chalk grassland, a globally rare habitat, is home to wildflowers and diverse range of butterflies and moths. Its wildlife includes burnt-tip, common and pyramidal orchids as well as Adonis blue butterflies, silver-spotted skippers and scarce forester moths.

The flora and fauna of Mount Caburn have flourished due to traditional grazing practices used for thousands of years across the South Downs. These management methods are still used to maintain the grassland today. The conditions required to create this habitat mean wildlife is particularly susceptible to human disturbance, so please remember to take litter home with you and to leave no trace of your visit. 

Getting there: Catch the Brighton to Eastbourne/Hastings train and get off at Glynde. Alternatively, for a longer walk, start at Lewes and head eastwards up Chapel Hill onto the South Downs.  

Thames Path National Trail 

Spanning 185 miles, the Thames Path National Trail passes through historic towns and cities, peaceful water meadows, bustling riverside communities and our capital.

Starting at the source of the Thames, to the west of Cirencester, the full 185-mile route crosses 8 counties and takes you all the way to Woolwich in East London. If you don't fancy the full challenge, there are plenty of great short routes along the way.

Enjoy a 9-mile stretch from Oxford to Abingdon: beginning at Folly Bridge, the route takes you past Christ Church Meadow and onwards past Iffley Lock and into the Oxfordshire countryside where the river passes meadows and farmland. Keep an eye out for waterbirds, such as kingfishers, and dragonflies including the Southern Hawker.

Another great spot to join the Thames Path is Henley-on-Thames. This beautiful Georgian town is a relaxed spot to enjoy riverside pubs and a laidback stroll along the river. Henley is also home to an interactive mural celebrating 30 years of the Thames Path which you can find at Mill Meadows Pavillion.

London has many starting points to offer, from leafy riverside nature of Richmond, the hustle & bustle and iconic views of the City, to the maritime history of Greenwich. Through London the path, mostly, covers both banks of the Thames so there are ample opportunities for creating your own circular route.

Plan your own trip, and find information on any diversions, by visiting nationaltrail.co.uk 

Getting there: For the Oxford to Abingdon route, catch the train to Oxford. To return to Oxford take the bus from Abingdon. 

For Henley catch the train from Twyford which is reachable direct from London Paddington and Reading. 

If walking the full route from west to east catch the train to Kemble and then the 882 bus to Smerrill Quarry,  a 30 minute walk from the start of the route. Return from Woolwich station.

If you are visiting the coast, rivers or other open water, check local conditions, weather and tide times, follow safety signs and choose a lifeguarded beach where possible. Consult with  Tide Times to help plan your visit, and read up on water safety advice before you set out. 

With the recent dry, hot weather, wildfire risk is high across the countryside. Please pack a picnic instead of a barbecue, take your rubbish home with you, and if you spot an unattended fire, get to a safe place and call 999.  

Remember to always follow the Countryside Code when you’re out and about in nature!

entry.title: Explore More for Less: Affordable Southwest Nature Days Out
entry.summary: If you’re looking for fun and accessible days out that are low-cost, then we have you covered. Not only is spending time in nature great for your wellbeing, it can also be great for your bank balance. Here are our suggestions for our favourite affordable days out in …
entry.content:
If you’re looking for fun and accessible days out that are low-cost, then we have you covered. Not only is spending time in nature great for your wellbeing, it can also be great for your bank balance. Here are our suggestions for our favourite affordable days out in the Southwest!

The Southwest is packed with incredible places to explore, many of them completely free. Whether you're looking for riverside strolls, family-friendly wildlife watching, rockpool adventures, rocky scrambles or spectacular wildflower meadows, there's plenty to discover.

For wildlife, history and hands-on exploration: The Avalon Marshes Centre and Somerset Wetlands National Nature Reserve 

The Avalon Marshes Centre is the perfect hub for a family day out. Enjoy a picnic near the wildlife pond and make use of the amenities – including a visitor information point, café and accessible toilets – as well as visiting the on-site museum and craft gallery. Throughout the summer, they host family friendly events that connect people with the wildlife and history of the site. From there, it’s a short walk to Shapwick Heath National Nature Reserve, a gateway to the Somerset Wetlands here you can follow pushchair-friendly paths or ancient tracks. Lucky visitors might catch a glimpse of the resident beavers or sparkling kingfishers and dragonflies. 

Getting there: The 668 weekday bus service connects the Avalon Marshes Centre with nearby towns and villages. It is also linked to Glastonbury, Street and Wedmore by quiet lanes and cycle paths. The centre is around 10 minutes by car from Glastonbury and has free parking on site with donations encouraged.

For a classic day out by the sea: Weymouth Beach, Dorset 

For a proper day at the seaside, this award-winning stretch of golden sand is perfect for building sandcastles and paddling in the gentle waves. A stroll along the sweeping seafront connects you to the King Charles III England Coast Path where adventurous visitors can extend their day with a walk. Head east from Weymouth for a challenging cliff-top climb and panoramic sea views, or head west for an easier walk towards the unique landscape of Chesil Beach and Fleet Lagoon, a rare habitat and the largest saltwater lagoon in the UK. 

Getting there: Weymouth station is just a short hop from the beach. Weymouth is also well connected to nearby towns by bus and there are plenty of car parks, including a park and ride service. 

For accessible trails across diverse wildlife habitats: Goss and Tregoss Moors, part of the Mid Cornwall Moors NNR 

Goss Moor features heathland, wetlands, pools and scrub habitats. A largely level seven-mile multi-use trail provides easy access for walkers, cyclists and families, with Tramper, equestrian, and cycle accessible gates.  

Home to some of the country’s rarest species such as lesser butterfly orchid, yellow centaury, marsh clubmoss and Cornish moneywort. The 29 species of butterfly and 18 species of dragonfly and damselfly include the nationally scarce small red damselfly. Dormice reside in grassy open areas and the reserve is a stronghold for Britain’s fastest declining resident bird, the willow tit. The moor is surrounded by medieval farms and the characteristic remains of tin-streaming and gravel extraction.

Getting there: The nearest train stations to Goss Moor are in St Columb Road and Roche. Bus services run close to the reserve from St Austell to Newquay and from St Columb Major to Bodmin. See the Tradeline SW website for details.  

For coastal adventures: Wembury and the King Charles III England Coast Path, Devon 

Few places combine coastal scenery and wildlife quite as well as Wembury. Managed by the National Trust and part of a voluntary Marine Conservation Area, Wembury Beach is widely regarded as one of the best places in the UK for rockpooling.  

At low tide, families can discover an extraordinary variety of marine life, including sea anemones, crabs, starfish and small fish hidden among the rocks. The Devon Wildlife Trust’s Wembury Marine Centre helps visitors learn more about the area's rich marine environment through displays, events and guided rockpool safaris (free or for a small charge). 

Beyond the beach, the South West Coast path, which has been improved and is now part of the King Charles III England Coast Path. Here you will find spectacular walks, such as the popular ⁠Wembury to Heybrook Bay Walk with views across Plymouth Sound and out to the iconic Great Mewstone island.  

Getting there: The No.48 bus runs from Plymouth city centre. The Yealm ferry (for foot passengers and bikes) runs between Noss Mayo, Newton Ferrers and Wembury between 1st April and 30th Sept. By car follow the A379 through Elburton, then signs to Wembury Beach. The car park can fill quickly so arriving early is recommended.

For wildflowers and butterflies: Pewsey Downs National Nature Reserve, Wiltshire 

The steep sunny slopes of Pewsey Downs are the perfect place to spot butterflies dancing among colourful wildflowers this summer. Keep your eyes peeled for the electric Adonis Blue fluttering past and keen noses might catch the rich scent of wild thyme and marjoram drifting on the breeze. With spectacular views stretching across to Salisbury Plain, you can also get up close to the Alton Barnes White Horse, one of the eight famous white horses still visible in Wiltshire today. These hills are not for the faint-hearted, however, so a visit here may suit families with older children more than little ones in buggies.

Getting there:  Pewsey Downs has a free car park near Alton Barnes village (Postcode SN8 4LU) and buses from Pewsey train station run to Alton Barnes, about one mile south of the reserve. 

For rocky scrambles and epic views: Ebbor Gorge, Mendip Hills 

Not far from its famous cousin, Cheddar Gorge, is the lesser known but equally impressive Ebbor Gorge. Paths wind their way through the dramatic limestone cliffs while small streams and rocky climbs make for exciting scrambling. Make it to the top and you will be rewarded with stunning views across the landscape. See if you can spot the willow bear sculpture lurking in the woods, representing the beasts that once roamed these lands, and the many fossils that have been found in the local caves. 

Getting there: There is a free car park at the gorge, which is locked at dusk (Postcode BA5 1AY). 

For an oasis in the city: Urban nature walks in Truro, Cornwall

For walks close to the city centre, Daubuz Moor offers riverside meadows, wetlands, wildflowers and woodland along the River Allen ideal for pushchairs, wheelchairs and short family walks. Coosebean Woodland has riverside paths, woodland trails and open green spaces. Visit Truro also has suggestions for stunning coast and countryside walks within 10 miles of Truro.  

Getting there: Daubuz Moor is a 5-10 min walk north from Truro Cathedral to the gate on Moresk Road. For Coosebean Woodland follow the riverside path upstream from near Victoria Gardens or cross the footbridge from Truro railway station. Gate at the end of St George’s Road. Or use Coosebean Lane for a pram- or wheelchair-friendly path.

A few more favourites 

We can’t mention everything so here are a few more of our favourite low cost, accessible places to visit in the South West this summer.

  • Dorset: Studland Bay and Godlingston Heath - a stunning stretch of heath and dune backing onto golden sands, right on the King Charles III England Coast Path, and reachable by the seasonal open-top bus from Bournemouth or Swanage. 
  • Wiltshire: Cotley Hill National Nature Reserve - a hidden gem of chalk grassland near Warminster, home to rare orchids and a Bronze Age hillfort, with Warminster's rail and bus links putting it within easy reach of public transport. 
  • Somerset: Bridgwater Bay - vast tidal mudflats and saltmarsh teeming with wading birds, sitting alongside the England Coast Path, and accessible by local community transport schemes from Bridgwater. 
  • Avon and Mendip: Chapel Wood NNR - a peaceful pocket of ancient woodland near Chipping Sodbury, rich in birdlife come summer, with Yate station and connecting bus routes offer
  • Cornwall: Lizard NNR – see the Natural Lizard website for events, walks and places to visit on The Lizard peninsula. Lizard Point has an accessible track and volunteer-staffed lookout point for seals and other wildlife. ing an easy approach from Bristol. 
  • Devon: Pebblebed Heaths and the Otter Estuary - for a stunning mix of heathland, wetland and coastal scenery. Accessible paths, viewing points and circular routes suitable for all ages make for a relaxed day out close to Exeter. For information visit Pebblebed Heaths Conservation Trust website.  
  • Devon: Yarner Wood, East Dartmoor National Nature Reserve - in England's first National Nature Reserve, enjoy a network of easy walking routes, including the 2km accessible Miles Without Stiles trail. Offering bird hides, a pond-dipping area, woodland artwork and peaceful picnic spots.  

If you are visiting the coast, rivers or other open water, check local conditions, weather and tide times, follow safety signs and choose a lifeguarded beach where possible. Consult with  Tide Times to help plan your visit, and read up on water safety advice before you set out. 

With the recent dry, hot weather, wildfire risk is high across the countryside. Please pack a picnic instead of a barbecue, take your rubbish home with you, and if you spot an unattended fire, get to a safe place and call 999.  

Remember to always follow the Countryside Code when you’re out and about in nature!

entry.title: Your land, your choice: how Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier can work for farmers and land managers
entry.summary: By Dougal McNeill, Principal Officer, Agri-Environment Delivery, Natural England This blog explains and breaks down the role of Defra, RPA and NE in the Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier process, while also discussing some of the benefits and challenges of the …
entry.content:
By Dougal McNeill, Principal Officer, Agri-Environment Delivery, Natural England

This blog explains and breaks down the role of Defra, RPA and NE in the Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier process, while also discussing some of the benefits and challenges of the scheme.

Farming is challenging and in uncertain times the challenges become more acute and the appetite for risk diminishes. The challenges posed by drought have been especially acute this summer with government announcing drought support for farmers earlier in August. Anyone who works with farmers and land managers knows that the decisions you face - about your land, your business, your livelihoods - are rarely straightforward. So, when a scheme like Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier (CSHT) comes along, I understand why the first reaction might be: is this worth the effort? 

I want to explain what Natural England is doing to make sure the answer is yes, if it’s right for your business.  As well as explain our roles.  

CSHT is a team effort 

Defra sets the policy direction and priorities for the scheme - how it fits alongside other options like the Sustainable Farming Incentive and Landscape Recovery. Defra's ambition is clear: CSHT should drive high-impact environmental outcomes, targeting the land and habitats where it can make the biggest difference. 

The RPA administers the scheme - managing applications, processing agreements and handling payments. They are also working to improve the application service over time making the process clearer and more straightforward.

Natural England's role is the specialist advisory one - our advisers work directly with farmers and land managers to assess what is possible on your land, help shape agreements that are genuinely right for your farm, and provide the expert, site-specific guidance that neither a policy document nor an online portal can replace. We also work alongside the Forestry Commission, Environment Agency and Historic England, where woodland, water and heritage are part of the picture.

The joined-up approach is what makes the scheme function, and we are committed to improving it further. 

What CSHT is - and what it isn't 

CSHT is not a one-size-fits-all scheme. It is designed for farmers and land managers who want to do something ambitious for nature on their land - whether that is restoring peatland, managing ancient grassland, supporting wading birds, or improving water quality along a river. It rewards you for the real environmental value your land can deliver, not simply for owning it.

It sits alongside simpler options like the Sustainable Farming Incentive, and it is not right for everyone. That is precisely why the advice we offer matters so much. We are not here to sign you up to something that does not fit your farm or your goals. We are here to help you work out whether CSHT is right for you -and if it is, to support you through every step.

The difference good advice makes 

Since the scheme opened for applications in September 2025, our advisers have engaged with over 850 potential agreement holders across England. More than 600 have received personalised pre-application advice, and 430 agreements are now live and delivering for nature.

What makes me proud is not just the numbers. It is the feedback we hear from farmers about what that advice actually meant to them.

One farmer told us:

"The most helpful information was a timeline provided by a Natural England adviser which explained the process of the pre-application advice and specific details on what was required at each stage. It gave specific information rather than a generalised overview, which doesn't help."

That says everything. Farmers need clarity and practical guidance — not general information that leaves them none the wiser. That is what our advisers work hard to provide. 

One farmer described the adviser relationship simply:

"Her enthusiasm for improving nature on the farm really energised us to do more, and we are pleased and proud to be in the first round of the new CSHT."

While another customer explained what the adviser partnership meant to them: 

"Without Natural England's help we couldn't have done all this for nature, and it has been beneficial for the health of our farm as well."

These are not exceptional cases. They reflect what happens when farmers and advisers work together, honestly and practically, towards a shared goal.

Being straight about the challenges 

I would not be doing my job if I pretended everything is straightforward. Demand for CSHT is growing, and our resources are under real pressure. A significant wave of expiring agreements is approaching and managing that alongside new applications will require careful prioritisation across Natural England, RPA and Defra collectively.

We are also working to find smarter ways to reach more farmers without reducing the quality of advice. New approaches — like simpler single-action agreements for species-rich grassland and working with partners to help prepare pre-application advice that Natural England then reviews — are part of how we plan to extend our reach. These are practical solutions, not shortcuts. The quality of the advice remains non-negotiable.

Looking ahead together 

We have already identified more than 800 farmers and land managers to receive pre-application advice in the coming months, and we are working centrally to coordinate larger organisations so they can apply more efficiently too.

Defra, RPA and Natural England are aligned on what needs to happen next. The scheme is improving, the relationships are strong, and the momentum is real.

But what matters most is the relationship with you. Our advisers are committed to working alongside you, to help you make the right decisions for your land and your business.

We are here to help with advice - not to add to your challenges, but to make it as straightforward as it can be.

See Defra Farming Blog and GOV.UK for more details: 

  • See Defra Farming Blog and how you can express your interest in Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier
  • CSHT Guidance

entry.title: Putting Nature at the Heart of Healthcare: My Reflections from Bristol
entry.summary: By Marian Spain, CEO of Natural England In this blog, NE's Chief Executive Marian Spain reflects on her recent visit to healthcare sites in Bristol to explore how partners are incorporating nature into health and wellbeing, and discusses Natural England's …
entry.content:
By Marian Spain, CEO of Natural England

In this blog, NE's Chief Executive Marian Spain reflects on her recent visit to healthcare sites in Bristol to explore how partners are incorporating nature into health and wellbeing, and discusses Natural England's role in this.

One of the moments that stayed with me from my visit to Bristol was sitting in the greenhouse in the community allotment at Southmead Hospital and hearing how this green space on a busy hospital estate has become a place of calm, connection and recovery for patients, staff and local people. 

It was a powerful reminder that nature is not a nice-to-have in healthcare. It is part of what helps people feel well, recover well and live well. 

Across my day in Bristol, I saw how partners are bringing nature and health closer together from a specialist mental health ward, to a community-focused GP practice, to one of the country’s largest hospital estates. 

For too long, nature and health have often been treated as separate issues. But the evidence, and the lived experience of communities across England, tell us something different. Access to nature supports our physical health, our mental wellbeing and our quality of life. In fact, 90% of adults in England say green and natural spaces are good for their mental health and wellbeing. 

That is why Natural England’s new strategy, Recovering Nature for Growth, Health and Security, champions creating healthier places for people to live, work and spend time.   

Nature is part of our health infrastructure 

When we think about healthcare, we naturally think about hospitals, GP surgeries, medicines and treatments. All of those are vital. But we also need to recognise the role nature plays in supporting health and wellbeing long before people need clinical care. 

A walk in a local park, access to a community garden, or time spent in a wildlife-rich green space can all make a positive difference to people's lives. Yet access to nature is not experienced equally. One in five households do not have access to a green or blue space within a 15-minute walk, with the greatest inequalities often affecting more deprived communities. 

At Natural England, we want everyone to have the opportunity to access and benefit from nature, whatever their postcode. We also know that healthy natural environments can strengthen communities, support economic growth and build resilience to climate change. That is why investment in nature should be seen as investment in healthy places and people.

Seeing what's possible 

What I saw in Bristol showed how this ambition can be translated into practical action.

At Blackberry Hill Hospital, Avon and Wiltshire Mental Health Partnership NHS Trust has incorporated nature into the design and operation of the new Kingfisher Ward, recognising the role that nature-rich environments can play in supporting recovery and wellbeing. 

At Charlotte Keel Medical Centre, partners including Alive Activities and the West of England Mayoral Combined Authority have helped transform an outdoor courtyard space, demonstrating how even busy urban healthcare settings can create opportunities for connecting with nature. Over lunch they described to me what a difference it makes to the quality of breaks at work for staff, and how the courtyard garden has supported patients, some of whom now volunteer their time to look after the space.

And at Southmead Hospital, North Bristol NHS Trust is showing how a major healthcare estate can work harder for both people and Nature through community allotments, green infrastructure and biodiversity improvements that support health, wellbeing and environmental outcomes.

Each project was different, but the message was consistent: when organisations work together, nature can become part of everyday care, not an optional extra.

What impressed me most was the strength of the partnerships behind this work. Across Bristol, NHS organisations, local government, public health teams, community groups and environmental organisations are collaborating around a shared vision. Through initiatives such as green social prescribing, nature-based health projects and wider place-based partnerships, they are demonstrating how health and nature objectives can reinforce one another. 

Better outcomes for people and nature 

What gives me optimism is that this is not a choice between helping people or helping nature. The most successful examples deliver both. 

Creating greener places can improve wellbeing, support biodiversity, strengthen community resilience and help us adapt to climate change at the same time. These are not competing goals. They are mutually reinforcing.

Research suggests that regular access to greenspace could reduce GP visits by 28% and save the NHS an estimated £2.1 billion each year. At a time when health services are under increasing pressure, this is a powerful reminder that prevention matters just as much as treatment. 

To support organisations looking to take practical action, Natural England has worked with NHS England and the Centre for Sustainable Healthcare to develop the Nature for Health Resource Hub, bringing together tools, guidance and case studies that help healthcare sites improve their green spaces. 

The people I met in Bristol are showing what that looks like in practice, with commitment, imagination and care. There is much we can learn from them. 

Our commitment 

Natural England's ambition is clear: we want nature to be part of everyday life for everyone. 

That means restoring nature, improving access to green and blue spaces, and working with partners across the health, planning, environmental and local government sectors to tackle inequalities and improve wellbeing. 

The examples I saw in Bristol show what is possible. The challenge now is to build on these successes and make them the norm rather than the exception. 

Find out more

Visit the Nature for Health Resource Hub: https://nhsforest.org/resources/

Discover Green Social Prescribing tools and resources: https://socialprescribingacademy.org.uk/resources/launch-of-green-social-prescribing-innovation-community/

entry.title: Fighting Fire with Nature: How Healthy Landscapes Reduce Wildfire Risk
entry.summary: By Ruth Waters, Regional Director for the North of England, Operations Directorate, Natural England The UK is facing a growing wildfire crisis this year, with prolonged hot, dry weather fuelling blazes across our moors, farmland and urban parks. This blog …
entry.content:
By Ruth Waters, Regional Director for the North of England, Operations Directorate, Natural England

The UK is facing a growing wildfire crisis this year, with prolonged hot, dry weather fuelling blazes across our moors, farmland and urban parks. This blog explores why wildfires are becoming more frequent and severe, the role climate change plays in heightening the risk, and the wider consequences for our landscapes and water supplies. It also sets out what Natural England is doing to reduce wildfire risk on its nature reserves, and how partnerships are helping to tackle the issue on the ground.

This year we are experiencing large scale wildfires devastating the UK’s landscapes, from our moors and dales to farmland and urban parks. Prolonged hot and dry weather has provided the ideal conditions for fires to take hold, which we have also seen in mainland Europe. France has declared their ongoing wildfire situation as the worst crisis to face the country since the Second World War.

What are wildfires and why have there been so many recently?

In the UK the term “wildfire” means any uncontrolled blaze on vegetation that needs action to extinguish. Virtually all wildfires in this country are caused by human activity, from the careless (e.g. negligent use of barbecues) to the deliberate (e.g. arson), as well as the inadvertent, such as agricultural equipment faults and “managed fires” (e.g. heather/grass burning) escaping control. 

Our own records show that there have been over 240 reported wildfires this year on our most precious sites –Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) – including a 1,500 hectares fire in the Peak District (including Dove Stone RSPB reserve) which has damaged moorland valued for its blanket bog and heathland habitats, as well as breeding populations of birds such as golden plover and merlin. This fire was started by people setting off fireworks – so far one person from Greater Manchester has been charged with multiple criminal offences relating to the incident. 

Most recently a fire at Dunwich Heath in Suffolk engulfed some 150 hectares, with the National Trust estimating it could take 25 years for the site to recover. At the height of the fire over 100 firefighters were needed to bring it under control, with hundreds of homes and caravans evacuated.

The consequences of climate change

Climate change is heightening the risk of wildfires. Extreme weather events are increasing, and like 2025, this summer has seen prolonged periods of dry weather alongside a series of record-breaking heatwaves across the world.

On 29th July, the Environment Agency announced that more than half of England was in drought. Looking more widely, Europe has warmed almost twice as fast as the global average. A warming atmosphere combined with prolonged dry conditions accelerates moisture removal from vegetation and soils. This creates an abundance of dry fuel for blazes to take hold and spread.

It’s not just the direct destruction from the fires themselves that we need to deal with. The bare, dry soil they leave behind repels water from the next rainfall event, causing run-off that can lead to soil erosion and flooding. In addition, sediment flowing into watercourses adds to the treatment costs for drinking water (over 70% of our drinking water comes from our uplands), which is then passed onto customers through higher water bills.

What is Natural England doing right now?

Reducing wildfire risks and impacts on our National Nature Reserves

As a landowner ourselves, we continue to put measures in place on our National Nature Reserves (NNRs) to adapt and respond to increasing wildfire risk.  We are responsible for the management of over 130 NNRs – not all are at high risk from wildfire, but many are and climate change will see more of our NNRs at risk of either accidental or deliberate fires. We have developed wildfire emergency plans for our high-risk reserves that have information that will help our staff and the fire service in the event of fire such as access points, key-holders and muster points.

We ensure staff on high-risk sites have received specialist vegetation fire training provided through LANTRA and the Forestry Commission, and that we have the specialist equipment available to support fire and rescue services and to fight minor fires ourselves.

We incorporate fire reduction measures into our core site management. This reduces the ‘fuel’ available to a fire. For example, using firebreaks of broadleaved woodland and vegetation management such as grazing and cutting to stop a fire from spreading.

We use more active restoration measures to give nature a helping hand, like stone dams or bunds to hold back water in our peatlands, keeping water in the landscape for longer. Maintaining fire breaks and access routes also helps move firefighting equipment to isolated parts of our estate.

Prevention is better than cure

On our most vulnerable sites during periods of high fire risk, we present a more active, visible warden presence, supported by signage and publicity. This isn’t just aimed at deterring those who start fires deliberately, but at reducing the risk from accidental fires caused by discarded cigarettes or glass bottles or people using disposable barbeques.

Experience has demonstrated that where we are able to provide a high-profile warden presence that engages with the public constructively, fire incidents are reduced. In extreme cases we can temporally reduce access to an area to protect the public.

Working in partnership

We work with partners across England on a number of wildfire issues.

Nationally Natural England administers the Nature for Climate Peatland Grant Scheme, working with landowners and over 100 partners to rewet and restore peatlands, which hold more water in the landscape making it more difficult for fire to spread. Natural England are also part of the England and Wales Wildfire Forum which works to expand understanding of wildfires to reduce the impact they have.

At a local level, Natural England is a member of the Dorset Heaths Partnership which has been exploring ways to tackle wildfire issues since 2007. The Partnership includes site managers, the Fire and Rescue Service and the police. 

The partners operate a WhatsApp group to both rapidly notify managers of a wildfire incident but also to coordinate water bowsers, equipment to cut and extend firebreaks and to advise the emergency services of site hazards and sensitive areas.

A dedicated partnership warden team works with local people, especially dog walkers, to rapidly report incidents and help engage with those that are unaware of the dangers of wildfire. Fire access points are all mapped and coded for ease of incident reporting and, more recently, QR codes have been added so the emergency services can get to the right locations quickly.

What Next?

A key finding of the latest adaptation report from the Climate Change Committee (CCC) - A Well-Adapted UK, is that coordination is lacking in a range of areas to manage the increasing risks to society from climate change. The report recommends the UK Government facilitates coordinated assessment and management of cascading climate risks between sectors and joint planning of the responses to extreme events (including wildfires).

At Natural England we have established a new Wildfire Project Group to co-ordinate the organisation’s work on wildfires, which is multi-faceted given our statutory duties as well as our landowner role. This group will review our procedures and ensure we continue to use the best available evidence to inform our decision-making and advice to Government. It will also consider our current approaches to more short-term wildfire mitigation measures, against the backdrop of our overall aim of recovering our ecosystems to bring long-term resilience to the growing challenges of climate change.  

Natural England is also working closely with Defra, the Forestry Commission and Environment Agency on a co-ordinated approach to wildfire planning and response, feeding up to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) as overall department lead for wildfire.

entry.title: Explore More for Less: Affordable East Midlands Nature Days Out
entry.summary: This summer, if you’re looking for fun and accessible days out that are low-cost, then we have you covered. Not only is spending time in nature great for your wellbeing, it can also be great for your bank balance. Here are our suggestions for our favourite affordable days …
entry.content:
This summer, if you’re looking for fun and accessible days out that are low-cost, then we have you covered. Not only is spending time in nature great for your wellbeing, it can also be great for your bank balance. Here are our suggestions for our favourite affordable days out in the East Midlands! 

 The school holidays are here, and the East Midlands has some special places to explore - many of them free or very nearly so. Whether you're after a coastal walk, ancient woodland, or a magical trail through the forest, there's something for every family this summer. Here are five of our favourite affordable days out in nature across the East Midlands.

Lincolnshire Coronation Coast National Nature Reserve 

Stretching for almost 30 kilometres along the Greater Lincolnshire coast, the Lincolnshire Coronation Coast National Nature Reserve (NNR), the first in the King’s Series of NNRs, is free to visit. The reserve brings together sand dunes, saltmarsh, mudflats and freshwater marshes of international importance, and is home to natterjack toads, grey seals, and a spectacular array of birds.

The reserve also forms part of the King Charles III England Coast Path (KCIIIECP), so you can combine a walk along one of England's great national trails with a chance to experience some truly special wildlife habitat. Cleethorpes and Mablethorpe neighbour the reserve, making it easily accessible and with plenty of options to grab some fish and chips before you head home!

Getting there: The reserve is accessible from several points along the Lincolnshire coast. Cleethorpes has a train station with regular services from Lincoln and Doncaster. Mablethorpe is accessible by bus from Lincoln.

Clumber Park, Nottinghamshire (National Trust) 

Nestled in the ancient forest of Sherwood, Clumber Park is a picturesque 3,800-acre expanse of parkland, heath, woodland and lake that was once the country estate of the Dukes of Newcastle. This summer, it's easier than ever to get there without a car, and cheaper too.

A new daily bus service links Worksop Train Station, Worksop Bus Station and Clumber Park, running every day from 25 July to 6 September 2026. Return tickets cost just £3 per person and include free admission to the park.

National Trust members, under-fives, and visitors arriving at Worksop by train with a valid rail ticket all travel free and enter the park at no charge. Under 16s are free from 1 to 31 August.

Once you're there, the National Trust’s Summer of Play programme offers six interactive play zones, free ukulele workshops, storytelling sessions and much more, all included with entry. This year also sees Clumber take part in a nationwide National Trust partnership with Pokémon, meaning there’s enough entertainment for children of all ages.

Getting there: Bus service operates from Worksop Train Station (served by trains from Nottingham and Sheffield). Return bus ticket (£3) includes park entry. Service runs daily 25 July – 6 September 2026.

Bradgate Park and Swithland Wood National Nature Reserve, Leicestershire 

Just a short journey from Leicester city centre, Bradgate Park is one of the region's most loved wild spaces. Spanning 438 hectares of rugged, ancient landscape, the park features ancient oak trees, roaming deer and some of the very oldest and rarest rocks on earth. The lower part of the park is accessible via a tarmac carriageway suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs, and the visitor centre tells the story of the estate's fascinating natural and human history. Both the park and the visitor centre are free to enter.

This summer, families can also take part in the Moths and Butterflies Trail, running until 23 August 2026. Follow the path from Newtown Linford to the visitor centre, spot painted examples of the moths and butterflies found at Bradgate and Swithland Wood, collect hidden letters and solve the mystery moth, then claim your sticker prize at the visitor centre. It's a lovely free activity for children of all ages.

Getting there: Newtown Linford is served by bus from Leicester city centre (Arriva service 120 from St Margaret's Bus Station). The park entrance at Newtown Linford is a short walk from the bus stop. Bradgate Park also has three car parks, charges apply.

Forestry England Sherwood Pines, Nottinghamshire  

Take a stroll into the deep dark wood for a day of adventure at Sherwood Pines. The forest is free to enter, with something for everyone: three waymarked walking trails, cycling trails for all abilities, and play areas throughout the woodland. 

Families with young children will love the Gruffalo sculptures dotted through the trees and the Room on the Broom interactive trail, where children can help Witch find her lost hat, bow and wand while exploring the forest. Room on the Broom trail packs are available from the visitor centre for £4.

Getting there: Sherwood Pines is near Edwinstowe, Nottinghamshire. The nearest train station is Mansfield (Robin Hood Line from Nottingham), with onward bus connections via the number 14 or 15 bus from Mansfield bus station (next to the train station). If driving, car park charges apply to non-members.

The Pennine Bridleway, Derbyshire 

For an accessible taste of Peak District scenery, head to Middleton Top, the southernmost start point of the Pennine Bridleway. This family-friendly, mostly flat trail follows the route of the old Cromford and High Peak Railway, and is suitable for walking, cycling or wheeling, making it a great option for families with pushchairs or wheelchair users. There's a visitor centre, café and toilets on site, plus a picnic area at the adjacent Redhill Quarry Nature Reserve. The historic Engine House is open some weekends (fees apply). 

Alternatively, further along the route, the picturesque village of Hayfield offers access to a short, one-mile stretch of the Sett Valley Trail, also following a former railway line through wildlife-rich woodland. The trail runs alongside the village bus station, with a handful of cafes, pubs and shops, plus a picnic area and toilets nearby.

If you'd rather see more of the Peak District without the walk, the Stagecoach Peak Sightseer open-top bus is worth considering. Running daily until 19 September, it offers hop-on, hop-off travel between destinations including Chatsworth, Bakewell, Castleton and Hathersage, so you can enjoy the views and dip into a village or two without lacing up your walking boots. It isn't a free option (a family day ticket costs £38), but it's a flexible way to see a lot of the National Park in a single day.

Getting there: Middleton Top is on local bus routes, with connections from Cromford, Matlock and Matlock Bath train stations. Hayfield's Sett Valley Trail runs alongside Hayfield bus station. The Peak Sightseer can be joined at various stops including Chatsworth and Bakewell. There are also morning journeys from Chesterfield train station and South Sheffield to Chatsworth with return journeys late afternoon. 

A few more favourites 

Of course, this is not an exhaustive list and there are so many more great places to get out in nature on our doorstep that we couldn’t possibly name them all. Here are a few more though which are family friendly and free to enter:

  • Whisby Nature Park near Lincoln (Lincolnshire Wildlife Trust) 
  • Attenborough Nature Reserve near Nottingham (Nottinghamshire Wildlife Trust) 
  • Frampton Marsh near the Wash (RSPB) 
  • Sherwood Forest National Nature Reserve in Nottinghamshire (RSPB) 
  • Sandilands Nature Reserve near Sutton on Sea (National Trust) 
  • Watermead Country Park near Leicester 
  • Allestree Park in Derby 

Or for some options even closer to home Local Nature Reserves are places valued for their wildlife or geology, designated by local councils for people to enjoy and learn from. Find your nearest one: Local Nature Reserves (England) | Natural England Open Data Geoportal

With the recent dry, hot weather, wildfire risk is high across the countryside. Please pack a picnic instead of a barbecue, take your rubbish home with you, and if you spot an unattended fire, get to a safe place and call 999. 

Remember to always follow the Countryside Code when you’re out and about in nature! 

The Countryside Code is a simple guide to helping everyone enjoy the outdoors responsibly while protecting the natural environment. It encourages visitors to respect other people, protect plants, animals and habitats, and leave gates, paths and property as they find them. By following the Countryside Code, we can all play our part in keeping nature accessible, safe and enjoyable for everyone, while helping to conserve the landscapes and wildlife that make our countryside so special.
